findings.title: Every replica of brupop-bottlerocket-aws/brupop-apiserver is on a selected node
findings.explanation: All 3 running replicas of this workload sit on nodes selected for maintenance. Taking those nodes together means the workload has no serving copy until replacements schedule and become ready, regardless of what its PodDisruptionBudget allows over time.

remediation.description: Split the nodes across waves so some replicas keep serving

limitations: Counts replicas by label-selector match, so a workload sharing labels with another may be counted imprecisely.
Does not model a rolling drain. Taking the nodes one at a time, waiting for replacements between each, may avoid this entirely — wave planning is out of scope at this milestone (ADR-0011).

findings.title: PodDisruptionBudget demo/web-pdb permits no disruption

evidence.note: the eviction API will reject every eviction while this is 0
as declared by the operator

findings.explanation: 1 of this budget's pods sit on the selected nodes, but the API server currently allows 0 voluntary disruptions. currentHealthy (2) equals desiredHealthy (2), so evicting any covered pod would drop the workload below its declared minimum. Every eviction will be rejected with 429 until this changes.

remediation.description: Raise the replica count so healthy pods exceed the minimum
remediation.tradeoff: costs additional capacity for the duration of the maintenance
reduces the availability guarantee the workload owner asked for; their call, not the maintenance operator's

limitations: Reflects disruptionsAllowed at the moment of the snapshot. A rollout finishing or a pod becoming ready can change it without any action here.
Covers voluntary disruption via the eviction API only. A node that fails or is deleted outright bypasses PodDisruptionBudgets entirely.

findings.title: Node ip-10-42-100-186.us-east-2.compute.internal holds more kube-system/coredns pods than the budget allows to be disrupted at once
findings.explanation: Draining ip-10-42-100-186.us-east-2.compute.internal evicts 2 pods covered by kube-system/coredns, but the budget permits only 1 voluntary disruption(s) at a time. A drain evicts a node's pods together, so it will stall partway through rather than fail cleanly at the start.

remediation.description: Spread the workload so no single node holds more covered pods than the budget allows
remediation.tradeoff: may require a topology-spread constraint or anti-affinity

limitations: Assumes the drain evicts this node's pods concurrently, which is kubectl's behaviour. A tool evicting strictly one at a time and waiting would eventually succeed.
disruptionsAllowed can recover between evictions as replacement pods become ready; this does not model that recovery.

findings.title: This maintenance removes every node in zone us-east-2a

calculation.formula: flagged when selectedInZone == totalInZone and other zones exist

findings.explanation: All 1 node(s) in zone us-east-2a are selected, so the zone leaves service entirely for the duration. Any workload whose replicas all sit in this zone loses every copy at once, and topology-spread constraints that require a pod per zone become unsatisfiable.

remediation.description: Take the zone's nodes in more than one wave

limitations: Whether losing a zone matters depends on the workloads in it. This check reports the topology fact, not its consequence.
Zone is read from the standard topology label. A node without that label is invisible to this check.

findings.title: Deployment brupop-bottlerocket-aws/brupop-controller-deployment has a single replica

evidence.note: no second copy exists to serve during the eviction
on a node selected for maintenance
minimum outage before a replacement can even begin

findings.explanation: Evicting this pod takes the workload to zero replicas until a replacement is scheduled and becomes ready. Termination alone allows up to 30s before the pod stops, and startup time is additional. A PodDisruptionBudget cannot prevent this — with one replica, any budget that permits a disruption permits a full outage. No PodDisruptionBudget covers this pod, so nothing will gate the eviction at all.

remediation.description: Scale to at least two replicas before the maintenance
remediation.tradeoff: requires the workload to tolerate running more than one copy

remediation.description: Accept the outage and schedule the maintenance for a low-traffic window
remediation.tradeoff: the outage still happens; it is only better timed

limitations: Does not measure how long rescheduling actually takes. The outage length depends on image pull, startup, and readiness probes, none of which are visible in cluster state.
A single replica may be intentional and harmless — a batch worker, a leader-elected component with a passive standby elsewhere. This check sees the replica count, not the intent.

findings.title: Aggregate CPU is sufficient after removing the selected nodes

evidence.note: leaving the fleet

calculation.formula: free = allocatable - alreadyRequested; shortfall = needed - free

findings.explanation: The evicted pods request 285m of CPU and 1570m is free across the remaining nodes. This clears the aggregate check only — it is a necessary condition, not a guarantee that the scheduler can place every pod.
limitations: This is an aggregate sum, not a scheduling decision. Sufficient total capacity does not prove any individual pod fits on any individual node: ten nodes with 1 core free each cannot place a pod requesting 4 cores. Only the scheduler can answer that.

Scheduler predicates are not evaluated. Node selectors, affinity, taints, topology spread, and volume topology can each prevent placement regardless of free capacity. Those are covered by separate analyzers, which have their own limitations.
Uses resource *requests*, which is what the scheduler uses. A pod with no request counts as zero here and can still consume a node's actual CPU and memory at runtime.
Cordoned and not-Ready nodes are excluded from remaining capacity, since they accept no new pods.
Cluster autoscaling is not modelled. A cluster that would add nodes on demand may absorb this fine.

findings.title: Aggregate memory is sufficient after removing the selected nodes

evidence.note: leaving the fleet

calculation.formula: free = allocatable - alreadyRequested; shortfall = needed - free

findings.explanation: The evicted pods request 212Mi of memory and 3Gi is free across the remaining nodes. Aggregate check only.
limitations: This is an aggregate sum, not a scheduling decision. Sufficient total capacity does not prove any individual pod fits on any individual node: ten nodes with 1 core free each cannot place a pod requesting 4 cores. Only the scheduler can answer that.

Scheduler predicates are not evaluated. Node selectors, affinity, taints, topology spread, and volume topology can each prevent placement regardless of free capacity. Those are covered by separate analyzers, which have their own limitations.
Uses resource *requests*, which is what the scheduler uses. A pod with no request counts as zero here and can still consume a node's actual CPU and memory at runtime.
Memory cannot be oversubscribed the way CPU can. A pod exceeding its limit is killed, not throttled, so headroom here is less forgiving than it looks.
